blocks.text: Of all the small fields scattered through a JSON-RPC message, id might be the least glamorous and the most load bearing.

It looks like an afterthought, a single number or string tucked into a request, but it is the entire mechanism that lets a client keep track of which question got which answer once many requests are in flight at the same time.
This topic is about that one field, where it is allowed to appear, what makes it valid, and why leaving it out changes a message completely.
1. What the id Field Is For

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A request with an id gets a response with the same id

blocks.text: The id field exists to solve one specific problem, when a client can have more than one request outstanding at a time, how does it know which response answers which request. The id is the shared label, chosen by the requester and copied back unchanged by the responder, that makes that matching possible.

Without it, a client with two pending requests would have no reliable way to tell two arriving responses apart except by guessing based on timing, which breaks down the moment one request happens to take longer than the other.

It is worth noticing that this is the only correlation mechanism JSON-RPC provides at all, there is no separate correlation header, no wrapper envelope, the id embedded directly in the message body is doing all of the work by itself.

Think of it like a coat check ticket, the number itself means nothing, what matters is that the same number is stamped on both halves, the one you keep and the one attached to your coat, so the two can be reunited later regardless of how many other coats are hanging nearby.
2. Where id Appears: Requests and Responses Only

id shows up in exactly two message types, requests and the responses that answer them. A request carries an id chosen by whoever sent it, and the matching response carries that exact same value back. Notifications never carry an id at all, which is in fact the defining structural feature that makes a notification a notification.

This is also the fastest way to classify an unfamiliar message, if it has an id and a method, it is a request, if it has an id and a result or error, it is a response, if it has no id at all, it is a notification, regardless of anything else in the payload.
3. Uniqueness Within a Session

An id only needs to be unique among requests that are currently pending within one session, not unique for all time, and not unique across different sessions or different servers. Once a response for a given id has been received and handled, that id becomes free to reuse for a brand new request.

This scoped uniqueness is what makes simple, cheap id generation, like an incrementing counter, perfectly sufficient, there is no need for anything as heavyweight as a globally unique identifier just to label a handful of requests that are alive at any one moment.

Two different sessions, even between the exact same client and server reconnecting a moment later, start fresh, an id that was in use in the previous session carries no meaning at all in the new one, since the new session has its own empty pending table.

This scoping is also why an id is meaningless without its session, showing someone a bare id value in isolation, with no session context attached, tells them nothing at all about what request it once referred to.
4. Who Generates the id

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The sender of a request generates the id

blocks.text: Whoever sends the request generates its id, since requests can travel in both directions in MCP, a server asking a client to run a sampling call generates its own id for that request exactly the same way a client generates one when calling a tool.

This means both a client and a server each maintain their own space of ids for the requests they originate, and there is no requirement that these two spaces avoid overlapping, a client can be using id 1 for its own request at the same moment a server happens to also be using id 1 for a request it sent the other direction.

blocks.title: id generation is never negotiated
blocks.content: There is no handshake step where client and server agree on how ids will be formed, each side is free to choose its own scheme entirely independently, since ids from different sides are never compared against each other.

blocks.text: A useful mental check when reading protocol traffic is to ask whose turn it was to speak first, whichever side sent the very first message of that exchange is also the side that chose its id.
5. Valid id Types: String or Number

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A string id is compared against a number id

blocks.text: JSON-RPC allows an id to be either a string or a number, MCP does not mandate one over the other, an implementation can pick whichever is more convenient, a simple incrementing integer, or a generated string like a short random token.

One type is explicitly disallowed by the specification, a null id, since null is reserved to mean something else in edge cases involving malformed requests, using it as an ordinary request id would create ambiguity.

blocks.text: Mixing types is also fine, a client is not required to pick one type and stick with it forever, a session can freely use 1, then "abc", then 2, the only rule that matters is that whatever value is chosen stays unique among currently pending requests.

Some implementations prefer strings specifically because they are easy to make visually distinctive in logs, prefixing them with a short tag like req or srv makes it immediately obvious, just from reading a log line, which side originated a given request.
6. Why Notifications Omit id

A notification has no response coming back, so there would be nothing for its id to ever be matched against. Including one would be pure overhead, a value generated, sent, and never referenced again, which is exactly why the specification defines a notification as a message with no id field at all rather than one with an id that simply goes unused.

This is also a useful lens for reviewing a new message type someone proposes adding to a protocol, if it would never need a response, it probably should not carry an id, and if it does need one, it was probably meant to be a request all along.
7. How a Client Tracks Pending ids

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A client tracks a pending ids map

blocks.text: In practice a client keeps a small table, a map from id to whatever is waiting on that request, a callback, a promise, or a future. When a request goes out, an entry is added, when a matching response comes back, that entry is looked up, resolved, and removed.

A production implementation typically adds a timeout alongside each pending entry, so a request that never receives a response eventually gets rejected on the client's own initiative rather than waiting indefinitely for a reply that may never arrive.

The size of this table naturally reflects how many requests are genuinely in flight at once, a client that sends requests one at a time and always awaits each response before sending the next will rarely see more than a single entry in it.
8. What Happens If an id Is Reused

Reusing an id while a request using that same id is still pending creates ambiguity, if two responses eventually arrive both carrying that id, the client has no correct way to know which one answers which call. This is a bug in the sender, not something the protocol resolves for it, so id generation should always check that a value is not currently in use before sending.

blocks.title: A counter that never resets is the simplest safe choice
blocks.content: An ever increasing counter for the lifetime of a session guarantees no id is ever reused while still pending, since old ids are never revisited at all.

blocks.text: This kind of bug tends to hide well in testing, since low request volume rarely produces an actual collision, and only shows up under real concurrent load, which is exactly why a safe generation strategy should be chosen from the start rather than patched in later.
9. What Happens If a Response id Does Not Match Any Pending Request

If a response arrives carrying an id the client has no record of, perhaps because it already timed out and was removed, or because of a bug on the server, the client cannot do anything meaningful with it beyond logging the oddity and discarding the message. There is no request left to resolve.

A well behaved client treats this as a signal worth logging rather than silently swallowing, a stray unmatched id can point to a real bug, a request that timed out too early, or a server that duplicated a response, either way it deserves attention rather than being dropped without a trace.
10. ids and Concurrent Requests

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Request A with id 1 and request B with id 2 run concurrently

blocks.text: The entire reason ids exist is to make concurrency safe, a client sending three requests back to back does not have to wait for each one to finish before sending the next, it can fire all three, and rely on ids alone to sort out which of the three eventually returned responses belongs to which call.

Without unique ids, a client wanting this kind of concurrency would be forced back into sending one request, waiting for its response, and only then sending the next, turning what should be a fast parallel batch of independent lookups into a slow, serial chain.
11. ids Are Not Guaranteed Sequential

While a simple counter naturally produces sequential ids, nothing in the protocol requires that, an implementation could just as easily generate random strings, and a client on the receiving end should never infer meaning, ordering, or anything else from the numeric or lexical value of an id, it is purely an opaque label for matching.

Some servers intentionally randomize their own outgoing request ids for no reason beyond avoiding any accidental dependency, in client or testing code, on ids happening to increase in a predictable pattern.
12. ids Do Not Need to Be Globally Unique

It is tempting to reach for a UUID out of habit, but a session scoped counter does the job with far less overhead, since the only guarantee actually required is uniqueness among requests that are simultaneously pending on one connection, not uniqueness across the entire universe of MCP sessions everywhere.

blocks.text: 13. Server-Initiated Requests Also Need ids

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A server-initiated request also needs an id

blocks.text: Requests are not only a client to server thing, a server can send a request to the client too, sampling being the most common example, and that request needs an id exactly the same way, generated by the server, and copied back by the client in its response.

A client responding to a server-initiated request follows the exact same rule as a server responding to a client, copy the id from the request into the result or error it sends back, the direction of the original request does not change how the id is handled.

This symmetry is one of the cleanest parts of the design, the rules around ids never change based on which side happened to originate the request, a response is a response, and matching by id works exactly the same way in both directions.
14. id Collisions Between Client and Server-Initiated Requests

Because a client tracks its own outgoing requests and a server tracks its own outgoing requests separately, there is no conflict even if both happen to choose the same id value at the same time, a response is only ever matched within the pending table of whichever side originated that particular request.

This separation by origin is why implementations typically keep two pending tables rather than one, a table for requests this side sent out, and implicitly, a separate acceptance of whatever ids the other side happens to be using for its own outgoing requests.
15. Practical id Generation Strategies

Most implementations reach for one of two simple approaches, an incrementing counter local to the connection, or a short random or UUID style string. The counter is cheaper and easier to reason about, the random string is convenient when several independent parts of a program need to generate ids without coordinating a shared counter.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Incrementing counter","Simple, cheap, trivially unique per session","Needs a single shared counter variable"],["Random or UUID string","No shared state needed to generate one","Slightly larger messages, more bytes on the wire"]]}

blocks.text: Neither strategy is objectively correct, the right choice usually comes down to whatever is easiest to wire up correctly in the language and runtime a particular client or server is already built in.
16. Debugging With ids

When something goes wrong in a session, logging every request and response together, keyed by id, is usually the fastest way to reconstruct what actually happened, since the id is exactly the join key that ties a problem report back to the specific call that caused it.

Many implementations log the full request at send time and the full response at receive time, both tagged with the same id, which turns a chronological jumble of messages into an easily filterable, per call history.

blocks.title: ids make replay and testing easier too
blocks.content: A recorded session of request and response pairs, matched by id, can be replayed against a mock server in tests, since the id is exactly the field that lets a test harness line up a canned response with the request it should answer.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Trace how a client keeps three concurrent requests straight using nothing but ids.

items: 1. Client sends tools/list with id 1, resources/list with id 2, and prompts/list with id 3, all within the same second, without waiting for any of them individually.
2. Client stores three pending entries, keyed by 1, 2, and 3, each holding a promise the calling code is awaiting.
3. The prompts/list response, id 3, happens to come back first because it required the least work on the server.
4. Client looks up 3 in its pending table, finds the matching promise, resolves it, and removes the entry.
5. The resources/list response, id 2, arrives next, then finally tools/list, id 1, arrives last, each resolved the same way.
6. All three calling code paths eventually receive their correct results, even though the responses came back in a completely different order than the requests were sent.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Reusing an id while a previous request using that same id is still pending, creating an unresolvable ambiguity if both eventually respond.
Assuming ids increase in the order responses arrive, and using arrival order to guess which request a response belongs to instead of checking id.
Sending null as an id, which the specification reserves and does not treat as an ordinary request identifier.
Forgetting that a server can also originate requests, and failing to generate and track ids on that side of the connection too.
Using a single shared id counter across multiple independent sessions, when each session should track its own ids separately.
Never cleaning up a pending table entry after a response or timeout, letting old ids and stale callbacks pile up over a long lived session.

blocks.text: Practice
Implement a minimal id generator and pending table wrapper that guarantees no id is ever reused while still outstanding, and safely handles a response for an id it does not recognize.
Key Takeaway

The id field is a scoped, opaque label, unique only among requests that are currently pending within one session, generated by whichever side sends a request, and copied back verbatim in the matching response so that concurrent calls never get confused with one another.
